::: {#sol-reversed-text-information}

@exr-forward-n-gram-conditional-entropy and @exr-backward-n-gram-conditional-entropy give each character away from the ends of the text
the same [conditional entropy](#def-conditional-entropy) forward and backward,
and @exr-reversed-text-total-entropy gives the whole text the same sum of conditional entropies forward and backward.
So the reversed text carries no more information per character than the text read forward.
The two games tie only on average:
in English, "q" is almost always followed by "u",
but "u" is rarely preceded by "q",
so a single guess can be easy one way and hard the other.

People find the backward game harder
because their guesses are worse,
not because the text holds more information.
A reader who guesses with a [probability mass function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pmf) $g$
in place of the true [conditional probability mass function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#def-cond-pmf) $f$
spends $\crossentropyf{f}{g}$ [bits](#def-bit) per character on average,
which exceeds $\entropyf{f}$ by $\kldivf{f}{g}$,
by the [decomposition of cross-entropy](source-coding.qmd#thm-cross-entropy-decomposition).
Years of reading forward make $g$ close to $f$ for forward guessing,
and no such practice makes it close backward.

:::
